summary.text: Constantinople, today's Istanbul, was the capital of the Roman and Byzantine empires from 330 until the Ottoman Empire took it in 1453.
Constantine the Great founded it in 324 on the site of the existing city of Byzantium, at first under the name Nova Roma, or "New Rome".
From the mid-5th to the early 13th century it was the largest and wealthiest city in Europe, protected by some of the most sophisticated defences of antiquity.

facts.label: Founded
facts.value: 324, by Constantine the Great, on the site of Byzantium

facts.label: Defences
facts.value: Proved impenetrable for nearly nine hundred years

facts.label: Everyday nickname
facts.value: "The City", or i Polis in Greek

items.prompt: A traveller wants to know why Constantinople grew so rich. What does the account point to?

options.label: It sat on the only land route into Italy
It was the gateway between two continents and two seas
It held the largest gold mines in Europe
It was the one port that the Persians left open

items.explain: The city's prosperity came from being the gateway between Europe and Asia and between the Mediterranean and the Black Sea.

items.prompt: A city has few soldiers and little stone to spare for defence. How did Constantinople's setting help its builders?

options.label: Mountains on every side made walls unnecessary
The river current washed away any enemy ships
Its Persian allies guarded the land approach
Water on its sides reduced the land that needed walls

items.explain: Its position between the Golden Horn and the Sea of Marmara reduced the land area requiring defensive walls, helping it build some of the most sophisticated fortifications of antiquity.

items.prompt: In everyday speech, people of the city just called it "the City", from a Greek phrase meaning "in the City". What came from that habit?

options.label: Its modern Turkish name
The name Byzantium
The title New Rome
The name Augusta Antonina

items.explain: The common phrase eis tin Polin, "in the City", was the source of the city's modern Turkish name, Istanbul. Byzantium was its far older Greek name.

items.prompt: Constantine first designated his new capital "New Rome", but it soon became better known under another name. Why that name?

options.label: It honoured Septimius Severus, who rebuilt the city
It came from the strait beside the city
It honoured the emperor who refounded the city
It marked that the city no longer belonged to Rome

items.explain: It became more widely known as Constantinople, meaning "city of Constantine", in honour of its founder. Severus's rebuilt name, Augusta Antonina, was quickly forgotten.

items.prompt: Picture the empire in the early 1400s, after the rise of the Ottomans. How much of its old territory was left?

options.label: Only Constantinople, its surroundings, and Morea, an enclave inside Ottoman lands
All of Asia Minor, with Constantinople as a distant outpost
Nothing, since the Ottomans had already taken the capital
A string of Latin realms divided among Crusaders

items.explain: As Ottoman power grew, the empire's territories dwindled until it was reduced to Constantinople and its environs plus the despotate of Morea, an enclave inside the Ottoman Empire.

items.prompt: Boosters of the city claimed that several of its hills matched the seven hills of Rome. What does this claim suggest about the city?

options.label: It was built on top of the old city of Rome
It was settled by people who had left Rome
It was built on purpose to rival Rome
It was a Greek colony older than Rome

items.explain: The city was constructed intentionally to rival Rome, and it was claimed that several elevations within its walls matched Rome's seven hills.
